pull.title: net: stop monitoring select exceptions outside Windows
pull.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
> 
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by ignoring the exceptionSet. Except on Windows, where we instead disconnect if its used.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). But this goes against the spirit of RFC 6093, as documented in the second commit.

net: stop monitoring select exceptions outside Windows

Windows needs select's exception set to detect failed non-blocking
connects. On other platforms, a TCP urgent pointer can leave the
exception set pending even when no data is readable. Only monitor it
on Windows, and disconnect established P2P peers if it is set.

Co-authored-by: Antoine Poinsot <mail@antoinep.com>

comments.body:
Should the below `if (recvSet || errorSet)` be revised as well? If we only set `errorSet` on Windows and we already handle it here, then the below can be just `if (recvSet)`.

Or, given that we only set `errorSet` on Windows, this `#ifdef WIN32` here is not needed.

@@ -564,6 +564,14 @@ std::unique_ptr<Sock> CreateSockOS(int domain, int type, int protocol)
 #endif
 
     if (protocol == IPPROTO_TCP) {
+        // RFC 6093 §5 ¶1 advises applications not to employ TCP urgent
+        // indications. P2P has no urgent-data semantics. The v2 encrypted
+        // transport treats TCP as a uniform byte stream; interpreting the
+        // cleartext URG flag as an interrupt would violate that design. P2P
+        // should never support such interrupts.
+        //
+        // RFC 6093 §6 ¶1 requires SO_OOBINLINE for applications that employ
+        // urgent indications. P2P does not, so leave SO_OOBINLINE unset.
comments.body:
This does not follow, and regardless that seems like a confusing comment to add here.

My reading of RFC 6093 is that it 1) discourages applications from sending urgent data 2) advises applications to set SO_OOBINLINE to fix the broken out of band mechanism regardless of their use for urgent data.

But regardless, i think that comment just adds more confusion than it clears up, and it would be better to drop it.

comments.body:
> 1) discourages applications from sending urgent data

The RFC says:

> Even though applications SHOULD NOT employ the urgent mechanism

This isn't about a misbehaving sender, but rather about application design (both sides).

> This does not follow

I'm not sure what exactly "this" refers to. It's true that the RFC does not forbid applications from setting `SO_OOBINLINE` if they don't "employ urgent indications".

I do think it's good to document that we don't "employ urgent indications". The absence of the setting implies it, but an actual code comment is more clear.

In any case, I'll drop the comment commit.
